newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Clash at Sierra Leone airport over secret radio.
newsitem.headline: Clash at Sierra Leone airport over secret radio.

text.p: Nigerian soldiers and forces loyal to Sierra Leone's coup leaders clashed on Wednesday at Freetown international airport, apparently over a radio station on which ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah broadcast.

The Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG, in a statement released in Liberia's capital Monrovia, accused the ruling military junta of attacking its forces at Lungi airport, which is across an estuary from the capital.
It warned that any further attack would be dealt with "ruthlessly". There were no immediate details of casualties.

"The junta launched the fierce attack on the allegation that ECOMOG installed an FM station in Lungi. The junta's attack was therefore aimed at destroying the station," it said, adding that the attack was repulsed.

The sound of the firing caused panic in the centre of the city, which has been jittery since a Tuesday clandestine broadcast by Kabbah stoked fear of a fresh attack by Nigeria. The whereabouts of the FM broadcasting station are unclear.

Freetown residents spoke of shellfire or mortar fire on Wednesday. Soldiers at strategic positions in the city told Reuters that Nigerian troops had opened fire to stop some Sierra Leone troops who tried to make their way to the airport.

Nigerian troops were in Sierra Leone under a defence pact before the May 25 coup but have been reinforced as part of West African efforts to reinstate Kabbah. Nigerian gunboats bombarded Freetown on June 2 in a show of force.

Sierra Leone's West African neighbours resolved on June 26, at a meeting of their foreign ministers in neighbouring Guinea, to press for Kabbah's return to power by dialogue and economic sanctions initially, but retained the option of using force.

"ECOMOG feels strongly that any further attack on its position will draw maximum retaliation," the statement said. "ECOMOG would deploy maximum firepower to contain it. In such circumstance, the rebel leadership should be held responsible for any casualties on innocent civilians."
ECOMOG is deployed in Liberia, where it is keeping the peace and helping organise national elections on July 19 to end seven years of civil war.
Sierra Leone rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the May 25 coup and flooded into Freetown. They call themselves the People's Army.
Military ruler Major Johnny Paul Koroma has named rebel leader Foday Sankoh, currently under house arrest in Nigeria, as his number two.
